title: [2407.20158] Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems

sections.heading: Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems

content.text: Predicting chaotic dynamical systems is critical in many scientific fields, such as weather forecasting, but challenging due to the characteristic sensitive dependence on initial conditions. Traditional modeling approaches require extensive domain knowledge, often leading to a shift towards data-driven methods using machine learning. However, existing research provides inconclusive results on which machine learning methods are best suited for predicting chaotic systems. In this paper, we compare different lightweight and heavyweight machine learning architectures using extensive existing benchmark databases, as well as a newly introduced database that allows for uncertainty quantification in the benchmark results. In addition to state-of-the-art methods from the literature, we also present new advantageous variants of established methods. Hyperparameter tuning is adjusted based on computational cost, with more tuning allocated to less costly methods. Furthermore, we introduce the cumulative maximum error, a novel metric that combines desirable properties of traditional metrics and is tailored for chaotic systems. Our results show that well-tuned simple methods, as well as untuned baseline methods, often outperform state-of-the-art deep learning models, but their performance can vary significantly with different experimental setups. These findings highlight the importance of aligning prediction methods with data characteristics and caution against the indiscriminate use of overly complex models.

Chaos is a ubiquitous phenomenon in nature and technology, arising from nonlinearities, complex interactions, or feedbacks within the system [[Ott02](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx19), [Str24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx32)]. Predicting the behavior of such dynamical systems is a critical goal in many scientific disciplines. Chaotic systems are characterized by their sensitive dependence on initial conditions, making them notoriously difficult to predict and posing a significant challenge to researchers studying them.

A traditional approach to addressing this problem involves using domain knowledge to model the dynamical system. However, this approach requires detailed understanding of the specific system that is often not be available. In recent years, system-agnostic, data-driven approaches have emerged as a viable alternative. These methods, which leverage techniques from statistics and machine learning, are trained on observational data to predict the future behavior of the system.

These algorithms range from relatively simple and computationally inexpensive methods, such as fitting polynomials, to highly sophisticated models that utilize complex neural network architectures, demanding significant computational power for training. To evaluate these approaches, various comparison studies have been conducted.

For instance, [[Han+21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx12)] focus on complex machine learning models with mostly classical neural network architectures. They do not include the sophisticated transformer model [[Vas+17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx33)], which has gained popularity due to its effectiveness for large language models. Such models are surveyed in [[Wen+23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx35)], where different variants of transformer models for time series forecasting are reviewed. Remarkably, [[Zen+23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx36)] demonstrate how simple linear methods can outperform these complex models. Additionally, [[Vla+20](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx34)] compare reservoir computers (RCs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), favoring RNNs, whereas [[SFC22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx29)] conduct a similar comparison, adding further machine learning methods and concluding that RCs are preferable.

Previous studies typically compare methods on a limited number of systems. However, [[Gil21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx9), [Gil23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx10)] emphasize the need to use extensive databases and benchmarks to evaluate the performance of different methods. They introduce a database of more than 130 different chaotic dynamical systems and, in their comparison study, find that the sophisticated NBEATS method [[Ore+20](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx18)] performs best. Hyperparameter tuning in this study is minimal, despite its importance for algorithm performance.

All in all, there is no consensus in the literature on which method should be preferred. Even a distinction in the quality of results between lightweight and heavyweight methods is not clear. Apart from using only a few systems (and often different data in each study), the lack of robustness of existing comparisons may stem from an inherent randomness in the evaluations. The results of the error metrics used may vary when different initial conditions are applied. If experiments are repeated only a few times with randomly drawn initial conditions, the results may still not be robust. If there is only one trial, then uncertainty cannot even be judged.

With this work, we aim to address several questions left open in previous studies. We compare various lightweight and heavyweight algorithms, including simple statistical methods that have shown promising performance but have received limited attention [[RH17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx23)]. We also present modifications of algorithms based on propagator map estimates, such as RCs, where we target the increment instead of the next state, and show the advantages of these for certain prediction tasks. We tune hyperparameters guided by the computational cost of each algorithm, allowing a broader exploration of hyperparameter sets for lightweight methods to facilitate a fairer comparison with heavyweight models.

As one source of synthetic data, we use the Dysts database of [[Gil21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx9)], allowing tests on a wide range of chaotic systems and direct comparison with the results in [[Gil23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx10)]. Additionally, we introduce a new database, DeebLorenz, which encompasses three variations of the well-known Lorenz63 system [[Lor63](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx17)], allowing for an easy comparison with other studies on the Lorenz63 system. Our database includes 100100 repetitions of simulated time series for each system to increase the robustness of results and to allow uncertainty quantification. The database also features a nonparametric version of Lorenz63 to assess the performance of polynomial-based fitting algorithms on non-polynomial targets. All the systems studied have state-space dimensions ranging from 33 to 1010, categorizing them as low-dimensional. Different observation schemes are used for each system to examine the impact of noise and time step intervals on performance. Furthermore, we propose a new error metric for forecasting tasks on dynamical systems, the cumulative maximum error (𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME}). It combines the benefits of integrated error metrics (as used in, e.g., [[Gil23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx10), [God+21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx11)]) and measures of forecast horizon, such as the valid time [[Ren+09](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx22), [Pat+18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx20)].

Our study demonstrates significantly better performance of various tuned and untuned simple methods compared to complex machine learning models on forecasting tasks for low-dimensional chaotic systems. Additionally, we find that the relative performance of methods is highly dependent on the experimental setup, though some trends, such as the strong performance of simple methods, remain consistent. Notably, introducing random time steps between consecutive observations dramatically alters performance. In this case, a Gaussian process-based method [[RW05](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx26), [Hei+18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx14)] that ranks mid-tier under constant time steps, outperforms all other methods.

The remaining parts of the paper are structured as follows: [Section 2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S2 "2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") describes the databases, the forecasting task, the methods compared, the 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} error metric, and the hyperparameter tuning. The results and key insights of the simulation study are described in [Section 3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S3 "3 Results and 10 Key Insights ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), followed by a short conclusion in [Section 4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S4 "4 Conclusion ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"). [Appendix A](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A1 "Appendix A The Databases ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") provides additional details on the databases, followed by a discussion of the estimation methods in [Appendix B](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A2 "Appendix B Methods ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"). Finally, additional tables and plots detailing the simulation study results are available in [Appendix D](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A4 "Appendix D Further Details of the Results ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems").

We use two different databases: DeebLorenz11 1 Differential Equation Estimation Benchmark – Lorenz, available at <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.12999941>, a database created specifically for this study, and the Dysts database22 2 <https://github.com/williamgilpin/dysts>, <https://github.com/williamgilpin/dysts_data> from [[Gil21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx9)]. An overview of their structure is given in [Figure 1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S2.F1 "In 2.1 Data ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), and further details are described below.

Both databases consist of solutions u:ℝ→ℝdu\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} of autonomous, first-order ordinary differential equations (ODEs), i.e., u˙​(t)=f​(u​(t))\dot{u}(t)=f(u(t)), where u˙\dot{u} is the derivative of uu and f:ℝd→ℝdf\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} is the vector field of the ODE describing the dynamics of the system. All considered systems are chaotic, i.e., they exhibit a sensitive dependence on initial conditions, an aperiodic long-term behavior, and a fractal structure in the state space [[Ott02](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx19), [Str24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx32)].

The two databases are complementary in nature. Dysts consists of many different chaotic systems with only one time series per system and dataset, and only a rather small amount of samples per time series. DeebLorenz focuses on different versions of the Lorenz63 system, using multiple different observation schemes and an order of magnitude more samples per time series than Dysts. This allows for a more detailed case study of forecasting chaotic systems, specifically using the Lorenz63 system, and enables the investigation of the effects of different settings under directly comparable conditions. As 100 time series per system and observation scheme are available with randomly drawn initial conditions, system parameters, and noise values, an evaluation of methods can be made robust in a statistical sense. To obtain any kind of robustness in the evaluation using Dysts, we have to aggregate over all of its different systems, which makes the results depend strongly and somewhat obscurely on the systems chosen for Dysts.

All three systems considered in DeebLorenz are related to the Lorenz63 system [[Lor63](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx17)], in which f:ℝ3→ℝ3f\colon\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R}^{3} is a sparse polynomial of degree 2 with 3 parameters. In Lorenz63std, the parameters are fixed to their default values used in the literature. In Lorenz63random the parameters are drawn randomly. In Lorenz63nonpar the parameters change with the state using a random nonparametric function drawn from a Gaussian process. See [Figure 2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S2.F2 "In 2.1.1 DeebLorenz ‣ 2.1 Data ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") for examples of ground truth data from these systems. Notably, Lorenz63nonpar introduces a novel approach to randomly sampling nonpolynomial dynamical systems, all of which appear to exhibit chaotic behavior.

The data are generated under different observation schemes: In all cases, initial conditions u⁡(0)u(0) are drawn randomly from the attractor of the system. For times t1,…,tn∈[0,T]t\_{1},\dots,t\_{n}\in[0,T], T∈ℝ>0T\in\mathbb{R}\_{>0}, the state u⁡(ti)u(t\_{i}) is recorded either directly as Yi=u⁡(ti)Y\_{i}=u(t\_{i}) or with random measurement error εi\varepsilon\_{i}, i.e., Yi=u⁡(ti)+εiY\_{i}=u(t\_{i})+\varepsilon\_{i}. The observation times tit\_{i} either have a constant timestep so that ti=i​T/nt\_{i}=iT/n or timesteps are drawn randomly from an exponential distribution ti+1−ti∼𝖤𝗑𝗉⁡(λ)t\_{i+1}-t\_{i}\sim\mathsf{Exp}(\lambda), λ=n/T\lambda=n/T. All combinations of these timestep and measurement options make up the four different observation schemes for DeebLorenz.

For each combination of the three systems and four observation schemes, the generation of the training data (ti,Yi)i=1,…,n(t\_{i},Y\_{i})\_{i=1,\dots,n}, ti∈[0,T]t\_{i}\in[0,T], with n=104n=10^{4} (in expectation if time steps are random), and of the (noisefree) testing data (tj,u⁡(tj))j=n+1,…,n+m(t\_{j},u(t\_{j}))\_{j=n+1,\dots,n+m}, tj∈[T,T+S]t\_{j}\in[T,T+S], S∈ℝ>0S\in\mathbb{R}\_{>0}, with m=103m=10^{3}, is repeated with different random seeds to create a validation dataset (10 repetitions) and a testing dataset (100 repetitions). Further details can be found in [Section A.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A1.SS2 "A.2 DeebLorenz ‣ Appendix A The Databases ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems").

The Dysts [[Gil21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx9)] database consists of 133 chaotic systems with dimensions between 3 and 10, observed with constant timesteps, i.e., ti=i​T/nt\_{i}=iT/n, and two different noise settings: one without noise Yi=u⁡(ti)Y\_{i}=u(t\_{i}), u˙​(t)=f​(u​(t))\dot{u}(t)=f(u(t)); the other with system noise, i.e., Yi=u⁡(ti)Y\_{i}=u(t\_{i}) with

where B⁡(t)B(t) is a standard Brownian motion and σ∈ℝ>0\sigma\in\mathbb{R}\_{>0} is the scale of the noise. For both observation schemes, data are available in a validation dataset and a testing dataset, which each consist of one repetition of generated training data (ti,Yi)i=1,…,n(t\_{i},Y\_{i})\_{i=1,\dots,n} with n=103n=10^{3} and testing data (tj,u⁡(tj))j=n+1,…,n+m(t\_{j},u(t\_{j}))\_{j=n+1,\dots,n+m} with m=200m=200 for each of the 133 systems.

For all systems, observation schemes, datasets, and repetitions, we impose the following task: Given the observations of the past, (ti,Yi)i=1,…,n(t\_{i},Y\_{i})\_{i=1,\dots,n} in the time interval ti∈[0,T]t\_{i}\in[0,T] (training time), and the true current state u⁡(T)u(T), predict the future states u⁡(tj)u(t\_{j}) at given times tj∈[T,T+S]t\_{j}\in[T,T+S] (prediction time) for j=1,…,mj=1,\dots,m.

Allowing the forecasting methods to know the true current state u⁡(T)u(T) — even in the case of otherwise noisy observations — eliminates the dependence of our simulation results on the (random) specific noise value of the final observation. This is crucial to increase the reliability of our comparison study, since prediction errors in chaotic systems typically grow exponentially with time. Additionally, it allows us to concentrate solely on the forecasting task (predicting future states) rather than on the data assimilation task (estimating the true value of a nosily observed state).

We apply and compare different statistical and machine learning methods on this task. The methods are described below in [Section 2.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S2.SS3 "2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"). For a given method, we first tune its hyperparameters on the validation dataset for each system individually: For each time series in the validation dataset, we train a given method and hyperparameter combination on the training data and calculate the error metrics described below on the validation data. We select the hyperparameter combination with the best (lowest) mean cumulative maximum error (𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME}, see [Section 2.4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S2.SS4 "2.4 Cumulative Maximum Error – CME ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems")), which creates the tuned method. Then, for each time series of the testing dataset, we judge performance the same way as in the validation dataset: We train the (tuned) method on the training data and create the predictions u^​(tj)\hat{u}(t\_{j}) for the prediction time. The predictions are compared with the ground truth u⁡(tj)u(t\_{j}) using different metrics.

In practice, the canonical discrete-time versions of these metrics are applied, i.e., integrals are replaced by suitable sums.

We apply a wide range of different methods. Additionally, for the noisefree version of the Dysts database, we also include the methods evaluated in [[Gil23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx10)] in our benchmark (pre-calculated predictions are not available for the noisy version). Names of these reference methods start with an underscore, e.g., \_NBEAT. In this section, we provide a high-level description of the methods specifically applied for this study. A more detailed description can be found in [Appendix B](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A2 "Appendix B Methods ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems").
The methods can be separated into propagators, recurrent architectures, solution smoothers, and other methods that do not belong to any of the first three groups.
We start with the last category, which also contains our baselines:

The recurrent architectures are similar to the propagators, as they essentially also estimate the propagator map PΔ​tP\_{\Delta\!t}. But instead of viewing the task purely as a standard regression problem, where the ordering of the data (Yi,Yi+1)i=1,…,n−1(Y\_{i},Y\_{i+1})\_{i=1,\dots,n-1} has no influence of the result, these methods keep an internal state that is updated while processing the data sequentially, ordered by time. The internal state influences the prediction of the next system state.

* • Esn\*: The Echo State Network (ESN) [[Jae01](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx16)] is a specific type of reservoir computer. It is similar to Random Features, but features of the previous timestep are also inputs for the feature calculation of the current timestep. This structure creates an internal state, allowing the ESN to retain memory of the information from previous inputs. * • Rnn, RnnT: The Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) [[She20](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx30)] has cyclic connections of neurons, allowing information from previous inputs to persist for future predictions. * • Lstm, LstmT: The Long Short–Term Memory network (LSTM) [[HS97](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx15)] is a variation of the standard RNN designed to capture long-term dependencies in sequential data by using gating mechanisms to regulate the flow of information and prevent issues like vanishing gradients. * • Gru, GruT: A Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) [[Cho+14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx4)] is a simplified variant of LSTM that uses gating mechanisms to control the flow of information, but with fewer parameters, making it more efficient while still addressing the vanishing gradient problem in sequential data.

The final category of methods are the solution smoothers [[RH17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx23), chapter 8]. In certain settings (that are slightly different from our experiments), these methods are shown to be optimal, see [[Sch24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx28), section 4] and [[SS24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx31), section 4]. Solution smoothers work in three steps: First, estimate u⁡(t)u(t) in the observation time [0,T][0,T] with a regression estimator u~​(t)\tilde{u}(t). Then, view the data (u~​(t),u~˙​(t))t∈[0,T](\tilde{u}(t),\dot{\tilde{u}}(t))\_{t\in[0,T]} as observations of (x,f⁡(x))(x,f(x)) and use a second regression estimator to obtain an estimate f^\hat{f}. Lastly, solve the ODE u^˙​(t)=f^​(u^​(t))\dot{\hat{u}}(t)=\hat{f}(\hat{u}(t)) on the time interval [T,T+S][T,T+S] with initial conditions u^​(T)=u​(T)\hat{u}(T)=u(T).

Similar to the 𝗌𝖬𝖠𝖯𝖤\mathsf{sMAPE}, errors are integrated over time, and similar to t𝗏𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽t\_{\mathsf{valid}}, the time and error of the worst prediction so far are essential for the value of the overall error metric. The 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} has many desirable properties:

1. (i) It is translation and scale invariant, in contrast to 𝗌𝖬𝖠𝖯𝖤\mathsf{sMAPE} and the version of the valid time used in [[Ren+09](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx22), [Pat+18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx20)], but similar to our definition of t𝗏𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽t\_{\mathsf{valid}}. This is desirable as every ODE system can be modified — without adding complexity — to create any translation and scaling of its solutions. Thus, the evaluation of an estimator u^\hat{u} should not depend on the location and scale of the system. 2. (ii) We focus on a task that involves evaluating the precise state within a near-future time interval, as in weather forecasting. In contrast, one could also consider a task where the long-term behavior of the prediction should resemble the ground truth, without emphasizing the error at any single point in time, as in climate modeling. For the former task, predictive power deteriorates quickly over time due to the chaotic nature of the systems considered. Therefore, if the prediction interval [T,T+S][T,T+S] is long, we are primarily interested in the early times when accurate prediction is possible. Accurate predictions at the beginning of the interval should not be discounted by divergence at the end, where accurate predictions are not possible anyway. This requirement is captured by 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} and, to some extent, by t𝗏𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽t\_{\mathsf{valid}}, but not by 𝗌𝖬𝖠𝖯𝖤\mathsf{sMAPE}. 3. (iii) The value of the 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} is always between 0 and 1, where 0 is only achieved by perfect prediction. In contrast, the scale of t𝗏𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽t\_{\mathsf{valid}} depends strongly on the system’s time scale and the best value t𝗏𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽=St\_{\mathsf{valid}}=S can be achieved for imperfect predictions. 4. Consistently, if all of the prediction is missing, we set the 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} to 11. 5. In contrast, for all values in [0,1][0,1] there is a prediction u^\hat{u} such that 𝖢𝖬𝖤m​(u^,u)\mathsf{CME}\_{m}(\hat{u},u) attains this value. Furthermore, u^1\hat{u}\_{1} and u^2\hat{u}\_{2} may have the same t𝗏𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽t\_{\mathsf{valid}}, but ‖u^1​(t)−u⁡(t)‖2<‖u^2​(t)−u⁡(t)‖2\|\hat{u}\_{1}(t)-u(t)\|\_{2}<\|\hat{u}\_{2}(t)-u(t)\|\_{2} for all t∈[T,T+t𝗏𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽)t\in[T,T+t\_{\mathsf{valid}}). If time is discrete, we can even have ‖u^1​(t)−u⁡(t)‖2<‖u^2​(t)−u⁡(t)‖2\|\hat{u}\_{1}(t)-u(t)\|\_{2}<\|\hat{u}\_{2}(t)-u(t)\|\_{2} for all t∈[T,T+S]t\in[T,T+S] while t𝗏𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽​(u^1,u)=t𝗏𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽​(u^2,u)t\_{\mathsf{valid}}(\hat{u}\_{1},u)=t\_{\mathsf{valid}}(\hat{u}\_{2},u). This cannot happen with 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME}: If ‖u^1​(t)−u⁡(t)‖2<‖u^2​(t)−u⁡(t)‖2\|\hat{u}\_{1}(t)-u(t)\|\_{2}<\|\hat{u}\_{2}(t)-u(t)\|\_{2} for all t∈[T,t∗]t\in[T,t^{\*}] for some t∗>Tt^{\*}>T and ‖u^1​(t)−u⁡(t)‖2≤‖u^2​(t)−u⁡(t)‖2\|\hat{u}\_{1}(t)-u(t)\|\_{2}\leq\|\hat{u}\_{2}(t)-u(t)\|\_{2} for all t∈[t∗,T+S]t\in[t^{\*},T+S], we have 𝖢𝖬𝖤⁡(u^1,u)<𝖢𝖬𝖤⁡(u^2,u)\mathsf{CME}(\hat{u}\_{1},u)<\mathsf{CME}(\hat{u}\_{2},u).
Let us also describe potential drawbacks of the 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME}.

The 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} is not symmetric, 𝖢𝖬𝖤⁡(u^,u)≠𝖢𝖬𝖤⁡(u,u^)\mathsf{CME}(\hat{u},u)\neq\mathsf{CME}(u,\hat{u}) in general, in contrast to 𝗌𝖬𝖠𝖯𝖤\mathsf{sMAPE}. But in our use case, the relationship between its two arguments u^\hat{u} and uu is also not symmetric. Thus, there does not seem to be a benefit to symmetry.

If uu is constant, then 𝗌𝖽⁡(u)=0\mathsf{sd}(u)=0 and ([5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S2.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ 3rd item ‣ 2.2 Prediction Task and Evaluation ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems")) is not valid. In this case, a reasonable definition is to set 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} to 11 for all u^\hat{u} except the perfect prediction u^=u\hat{u}=u in which case 00 is the appropriate value. Note that t𝗏𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽t\_{\mathsf{valid}} (and to some extent 𝗌𝖬𝖠𝖯𝖤\mathsf{sMAPE}) also suffers from this division by zero-problem.

If a prediction gets far away from u⁡(t)u(t) but recovers at a later point in time, the recovery is not accredited in 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME}. As future states in our dynamical systems are independent of the past given the present (Markov property), a time point with a good forecast following a previous time point with a poor forecast should be considered spurious and attributed to chance rather than skill. This is especially true in chaotic systems, where the dependence of the future on the present is particularly strong. But note that the same distance δ=‖u^​(t0)−u⁡(t0)‖2\delta=\|\hat{u}(t\_{0})-u(t\_{0})\|\_{2} can translate to different future predictability at times t>t0t>t\_{0} for different states u⁡(t0)=x1u(t\_{0})=x\_{1} or u⁡(t0)=x2u(t\_{0})=x\_{2}, x1≠x2x\_{1}\neq x\_{2}. I.e., we can have

On one hand, the value 11 in the min\min-term of ([5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S2.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ 3rd item ‣ 2.2 Prediction Task and Evaluation ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems")) could be replaced by a threshold parameter κ\kappa as in t𝗏𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽t\_{\mathsf{valid}}, removing the advantage of being parameter-free for the 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME}. On the other hand, κ=1\kappa=1 is a natural choice for the 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} (in contrast to t𝗏𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽t\_{\mathsf{valid}}), as the trivial baseline ConstM, u^​(t)=1n​∑i=1nYi\hat{u}(t)=\frac{1}{n}\sum\_{i=1}^{n}Y\_{i}, achieves ‖u^​(s)−u⁡(s)‖2/𝗌𝖽⁡(u)=1\left\|\hat{u}(s)-u(s)\right\|\_{2}/\mathsf{sd}(u)=1 on average. Furthermore, for every constant prediction there is a finite time point s0s\_{0} such that ‖u^​(s)−u⁡(s)‖2/𝗌𝖽⁡(u)≥κ\left\|\hat{u}(s)-u(s)\right\|\_{2}/\mathsf{sd}(u)\geq\kappa for κ=1\kappa=1, and κ=1\kappa=1 is the largest value with this property.

The value of the 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} depends on the testing duration SS (similar to 𝗌𝖬𝖠𝖯𝖤\mathsf{sMAPE}, but in contrast to t𝗏𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽t\_{\mathsf{valid}}). This could be mitigated by setting S=∞S=\infty and multiplying the integrand in ([5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S2.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ 3rd item ‣ 2.2 Prediction Task and Evaluation ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems")) by a weighting function w⁡(t−T)w(t-T), e.g., w⁡(τ)=exp⁡(−α​τ)w(\tau)=\exp(-\alpha\tau), but this introduces a new parameter choice α∈ℝ>0\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\_{>0}. To make the weighting choice-free and time-scale adaptive, α\alpha needs to be set depending on uu, e.g., to the inverse correlation time.

Each pair of a dynamical system and an observation scheme comes as a validation dataset and a testing dataset. For hyperparameter tuning only the validation dataset is used. Each such dataset consists of 11 (Dysts) or 1010 (DeebLorenz) repetitions/time series. Each repetition consists of training and validation data.

For a given method u^𝐚\hat{u}\_{\mathbf{a}} with hyperparameters 𝐚\mathbf{a}, we train it, predict, and calculate the 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} for different 𝐚\mathbf{a}. Let us denote the average 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} of all repetitions by 𝖢𝖬𝖤⁡(𝐚)\mathsf{CME}(\mathbf{a}) and the best hyperparameters among the tested ones as 𝐚∗=arg​min𝐚⁡𝖢𝖬𝖤​(𝐚)\mathbf{a}^{\*}=\argmin\_{\mathbf{a}}\mathsf{CME}(\mathbf{a}). Then u^𝐚∗\hat{u}\_{\mathbf{a}^{\*}} is applied to the testing dataset for the final results presented in [Section 3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S3 "3 Results and 10 Key Insights ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"). See [Appendix B](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A2 "Appendix B Methods ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") for a description of the tuned hyperparameters for each method.

To decide which hyperparameters 𝐚\mathbf{a} to evaluate, we follow a local grid search procedure: For a given estimation method, decide on which parameters should be tuned 𝐚=(a1,…,aℓ)\mathbf{a}=(a\_{1},\dots,a\_{\ell}). Each parameter aja\_{j} has a domain of possible values 𝒜j\mathcal{A}\_{j}. The domain can be categorical or scalar. For categorical parameters, decide whether they are persistent (always evaluate all options) or yielding (only evaluate best). For scalar parameters, decide on a linear or exponential scale and a stepsize sj∈ℝ>0s\_{j}\in\mathbb{R}\_{>0}. Decide on finite sets of initial hyperparameter values A0,jA\_{0,j}. Now, for step k∈ℕ0k\in\mathbb{N}\_{0} in the optimization procedure, evaluate all elements of the grid of hyperparameters (a1,…,aℓ)∈Ak,1×⋯×Ak,ℓ(a\_{1},\dots,a\_{\ell})\in A\_{k,1}\times\dots\times A\_{k,\ell} that have not been evaluated before. If there are none, stop the search. Denote the best hyperparameter combination evaluated so far as (ak,1∗,…,ak,ℓ∗)(a\_{k,1}^{\*},\dots,a\_{k,\ell}^{\*}). Generate Ak+1,jA\_{k+1,j} from ak,j∗a\_{k,j}^{\*} as follows: If the jj-th variable is categorical, set Ak+1,j=A0,jA\_{k+1,j}=A\_{0,j} for persistent parameters and Ak+1,j={ak,j∗}A\_{k+1,j}=\{a\_{k,j}^{\*}\} for yielding ones. If the jj-th variable is scalar, set Ak+1,j={ak,j∗−sj,ak,j∗,ak,j∗+sj}∩𝒜jA\_{k+1,j}=\{a\_{k,j}^{\*}-s\_{j},a\_{k,j}^{\*},a\_{k,j}^{\*}+s\_{j}\}\cap\mathcal{A}\_{j} if it has a linear scale and Ak+1,j={ak,j∗/sj,ak,j∗,sj​ak,j∗}∩𝒜jA\_{k+1,j}=\{a\_{k,j}^{\*}/s\_{j},a\_{k,j}^{\*},s\_{j}a\_{k,j}^{\*}\}\cap\mathcal{A}\_{j} if the scale is exponential.

The local grid search finds locally optimal hyperparameter combinations with a reasonable amount of evaluations assuming the number of tuned hyperparameters ℓ\ell is small enough. In this study, the algorithm is applied to ℓ≤4\ell\leq 4 hyperparameters to limit the computational costs. We tune more parameters in case of methods with low computational demand and limit to one categorical variable (no adaptive search) for the most expensive methods. See the main results [Tables 3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S3.T3 "In 3 Results and 10 Key Insights ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3 Results and 10 Key Insights ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") and [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3 Results and 10 Key Insights ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") in the next section (column Tune) for the computational cost of hyperparameter tuning. By adjusting the number of evaluated hyperparameters, we try to make the comparison fairer regarding total computational costs. The resulting total compute time can still be rather different between methods. This is partially due to the adaptive nature of the local grid search algorithm (i.e., the total number of predictions cannot be known beforehand) and partially due to the lack of meaningful tunable hyperparameters for some methods (in particular for very simple methods that typically have low computational costs). Furthermore, perfect fairness does not seem achievable, as the choice of hyperparameters to be tuned, the choice of initial hyperparameters, and the design of the scales all influence the result.

In contrast to our approach, [[Gil23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx10)] tune one hyperparameter for each method, independent of computational cost. The parameter selected is always related to the number of past time series elements that are inputs for the prediction of the next step. Note that in theory only the current state is required to predict a future state (Markov property) if there is no measurement noise, and as long as one has access to all system variables.

In all settings, almost all of the best methods (top 5) are comparably simple (e.g., [SpPo](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodsppo "4th item ‣ 4th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), [LinS](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodlin "2nd item ‣ 2nd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), [EsnS](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodesn "1st item ‣ 1st item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems")) and have low computational costs, as they do not rely on gradient descent learning. In contrast, computationally more complex learning methods (e.g., [Node\*](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodnode "4th item ‣ 4th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), [Trafo](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodtrafo "5th item ‣ 5th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), [Rnn](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodrnn "2nd item ‣ 2nd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems")) perform rather poorly. The only exceptions are [Gru](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodgru "4th item ‣ 4th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") and [Trafo](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodtrafo "5th item ‣ 5th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") for the noisy Dysts data and [Node1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodnode "4th item ‣ 4th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") for Lorenz63random and Lorenz63nonpar in the noisy setting with random time steps. Nonetheless, in these select cases, simple methods with similar or better performance are also available. See also [Figure 4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S3.F4 "In 3 Results and 10 Key Insights ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") for an illustration of this distinction on Lorenz63random with constant timestep. Furthermore, [Table 19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A4.T19 "In Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") shows that lightweight methods also outperform heavyweight methods under different sample sizes (at least on the system Lorenz63std with constant timestep).

Even some of the tuning-free methods ([SpPo2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodsppon "5th item ‣ 5th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), [SpPo4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodsppon "5th item ‣ 5th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), [PwNn](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodpwnn "1st item ‣ 1st item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), [SpNn](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodspnn "2nd item ‣ 2nd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), [LinPo4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodlinpo "3rd item ‣ 3rd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), [LinPo6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodlinpo "3rd item ‣ 3rd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems")) have mostly lower errors than heavyweight algorithms. We recommend using at least some of these methods as baselines for tasks similar to those shown in this study, as these methods are conceptually simple, easy to implement, have negligible computational costs, and good performance.

Altogether, performance, computational demand, and implementation complexity clearly favor lightweight methods. This calls into question the use of complex machine learning algorithms for the prediction of low-dimensional chaotic dynamical systems.

children.heading: 3.2 Polynomial Fits to Noisefree Data Are Accurate Emulators

content.text: [LinPo6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodlinpo "3rd item ‣ 3rd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") applied to the noisefree data of Lorenz63std delivers near-perfect forecasts, achieving a 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} of 6.6⋅10−66.6\cdot 10^{-6} (see [Table 7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A4.T7 "In Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems")). This method employs a degree-6 polynomial to approximate the propagator map u⁡(t)↦u⁡(t+Δ​t)u(t)\mapsto u(t+\Delta\!t). Our results are in line with the experiments on the Lorenz63 system shown in [[Gau+21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx8)] from which [LinS](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodlin "2nd item ‣ 2nd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") (fitting polynomial propagator with time-delay) is adapted, even though [LinPo6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodlinpo "3rd item ‣ 3rd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") does not use time delay. [LinS](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodlin "2nd item ‣ 2nd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") achieves a 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} of 1.9⋅10−41.9\cdot 10^{-4} in our setting.

While the vector field ff of the ODE in Lorenz63std is a degree-2 polynomial, the propagator map itself is not necessarily polynomial. However, since the propagator is derived from solving an ODE with smooth vector field, it is a smooth function. Taylor’s theorem ensures that polynomials can provide increasingly accurate approximations to such smooth functions. Note that we obtain our ground truth trajectory u⁡(t)u(t) using a 4th order Runge-Kutta solver with constant solver timestep Δ​t/10\Delta\!t/10, where Δ​t\Delta\!t is the observation timestep, to ensure the higher order terms are present in u⁡(t)u(t). If we were to use the Euler method with solver timestep equal to Δ​t\Delta\!t instead, the propagator would indeed be a degree-2 polynomial.

In [Figure 5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S3.F5 "In 3.2 Polynomial Fits to Noisefree Data Are Accurate Emulators ‣ 3 Results and 10 Key Insights ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), we demonstrate that [LinPo6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodlinpo "3rd item ‣ 3rd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") performs essentially as well as directly solving the ODE for Lorenz63std starting from initial conditions specified with 9 significant digits. This shows that [LinPo6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodlinpo "3rd item ‣ 3rd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") surpasses the accuracy of 32-bit single-precision machine arithmetic, which provides between 7 and 8 significant digits of accuracy. Moreover, as our simulation study stores data in CSV files with only 8 digits written after the decimal point, [LinPo6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodlinpo "3rd item ‣ 3rd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") is close to achieving the best possible accuracy given the limitations of the data (for noisefree Lorenz63std).

children.heading: 3.3 Method Selection and Hyperparameter Optimization Are Essential

content.text: Compared to the results of [[Gil23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx10)] (the method names starting with an underscore in [Table 3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S3.T3 "In 3 Results and 10 Key Insights ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems")), several of the methods considered here have much lower errors: For the noisefree Dysts data, the median 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} of \_NBEAT, the best performing method in [[Gil23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx10)], is 0.56. The lowest error achieved in our simulations is 0.0041 ([SpPo](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodsppo "4th item ‣ 4th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), [Table 14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A4.T14 "In Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems")).

One reason for the improved performance is the more extensive hyperparameter tuning in our study compared to [[Gil23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx10)], where only a single parameter was optimized for each method. For methods with low computational costs, we optimize several parameters. To illustrate the effect, we compare the median 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} (in parenthesis) for selected methods on the noisefree testing dataset from Dysts, as shown in [Table 3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S3.T3 "In 3 Results and 10 Key Insights ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") and [Table 14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A4.T14 "In Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"): The Nonlinear Vector Autoregression \_Nvar (0.80) and the Echo State Network \_Esn (0.79) from [[Gil23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx10)] are essentially the same as our [LinS](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodlin "2nd item ‣ 2nd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") (0.0054) and [EsnS](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodesn "1st item ‣ 1st item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") (0.030), respectively. Our simulations yield a median 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} that is orders of magnitude lower than for the corresponding methods in [[Gil23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx10)]. This indicates that optimizing key hyperparameters is critical for achieving good performance in these methods.

But note that [SpPo4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodsppon "5th item ‣ 5th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") and [LinPo4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodlinpo "3rd item ‣ 3rd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") are tuning-free methods and achieve median 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME}’s of 0.0079 and 0.040, respectively. Furthermore, from all methods of [[Gil23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx10)], only \_NBEAT outperforms the baseline method [Analog](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodanalog "3rd item ‣ 3rd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"). This highlights the critical role of selecting appropriate methods and baselines for a given task.

children.heading: 3.4 Noise and Timestep Design Influence Absolute and Relative Performance

content.text: In the absence of noise, forecasting becomes an interpolation task, whereas noisy observations yield a regression problem. Generally, as expected, performance degrades across methods strongly when noise is added to the observations. Moreover, methods that are best for the noisefree interpolation task are typically not the best for the noisy regression task. This distinction is evident when comparing the noisefree and noisy columns in [Tables 1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S3.T1 "In 3 Results and 10 Key Insights ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3 Results and 10 Key Insights ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") and [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 3 Results and 10 Key Insights ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems").

The Echo State Network [Esn\*](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodesn "1st item ‣ 1st item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") has access to states of the past, whereas the otherwise similar method Random Features [RaFe\*](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodrafe "4th item ‣ 4th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") does not. Because of the Markovian nature of our dynamical systems, knowledge of the past is not required in the noisefree case as the next state is equal to the (true) propagator applied to the current state. This is reflected in our simulation results, where [RaFe\*](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodrafe "4th item ‣ 4th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") tends to perform better than [Esn\*](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodesn "1st item ‣ 1st item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") in noisefree settings and vice versa for the settings with measurement noise. As the noisy systems of Dysts are created with system noise, they are Markovian. Surprisingly, the [Esn\*](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodesn "1st item ‣ 1st item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") seems to be at an advantage over [RaFe\*](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodrafe "4th item ‣ 4th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") here, too.

Under noise, the lower degree polynomial solution smoother [SpPo2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodsppon "5th item ‣ 5th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") performs relatively better than the higher degree polynomial [SpPo4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodsppon "5th item ‣ 5th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), and vice versa in the noisefree case. Overfitting to noise, which cannot happen in the noisefree case, seems to be the reason for this observation.

There is a noticeable difference in performances of methods between fixed and random timesteps ([Tables 1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S3.T1 "In 3 Results and 10 Key Insights ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") and [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3 Results and 10 Key Insights ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems")). Generally, random timesteps for the training data make forecasting (at fixed timesteps) more difficult. But also the ranking of methods according to their 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} changes: The Gaussian process based method [GpGp](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodgpgp "7th item ‣ 7th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") takes the lead for random timesteps. For fixed timesteps, this method is only mediocre.

As expected, propagator methods that do not have the timestep as an input, do not fare well if the timestep is not constant. With the additional knowledge of the timestep (\*ST and \*DT), the performance improves ([Table 15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A4.T15 "In Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems")).

The combination of a random timestep with noisy observations seems to make the learning task extremely difficult. In the case of Lorenz63random, only [GpGp](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodgpgp "7th item ‣ 7th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") (Gaussian process based solution smoother) and [LinST](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodlin "2nd item ‣ 2nd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") (ridge regression fit of polynomial propagator) have better scores than the baseline [Analog](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodanalog "3rd item ‣ 3rd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"). For Lorenz63nonpar no method beats [Analog](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodanalog "3rd item ‣ 3rd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems").

children.heading: 3.5 Repeating Experiments is Crucial for a Robust Evaluation

content.text: As there is only one time series per system available in the Dysts database, reported differences between the performance of methods might not be robust on the same system. Furthermore, confidence intervals based on the results on the 133 systems are hard to justify as one typically has to assume an independent, identical distribution of the considered values, whereas the selection of the specific systems for Dysts was a deterministic non-independent process. But note that the code for generating more data for Dysts is available at the respective repository.

In contrast, for DeebLorenz, experiments for the same system and observation scheme are repeated 100 times with randomly drawn initial conditions, noise values, and timesteps (if applicable). This allows us to judge whether reported differences in 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} values are statistically significant. In [Figure 7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A4.F7 "In Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), we visualize the results of paired tt-Tests for the null hypothesis 𝖢𝖬𝖤⁡(Method1)≥𝖢𝖬𝖤⁡(Method2)\mathsf{CME}(\text{{Method1}})\geq\mathsf{CME}(\text{{Method2}}). If the null can be rejected, it shows that Method1 is significantly better Method2 on the given system with the given observation scheme using the 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} as error metric. We see that the ranking of the algorithms as shown in [Table 10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A4.T10 "In Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") is mostly robust up to permutation of two or three consecutive ranks. In comparison, [Figure 8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A4.F8 "In Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") shows that only 10 repetitions would yield largely indistinguishable performances.
All in all, it seems prudent to repeat experiments to obtain more reliable results and be able to judge the confidence of these results.

children.heading: 3.6 Evaluation Lacks Robustness When Only Assessing a Fixed System

content.text: Although Lorenz63std and Lorenz63random share the same functional form of the vector field ff, differing only in their polynomial coefficients, the absolute errors and relative rankings of methods vary significantly between the two systems ([Tables 1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S3.T1 "In 3 Results and 10 Key Insights ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") and [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3 Results and 10 Key Insights ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems")).

Tuning for Lorenz63random (and Lorenz63nonpar) is hard in that the tuned hyperparameters must perform well across varying, randomly chosen system parameters. In contrast, Lorenz63std has fixed dynamics, allowing not only the functional form of ff but also the specific polynomial coefficients to be (partially) inferred during tuning.
Thus, a low error value for Lorenz63random is a more robust indicator of a method’s ability to generalize than a low error value for Lorenz63std.

children.heading: 3.7 The Functional Form of a Parametric Method Should Fit the System

content.text: Most systems in Dysts and all systems but Lorenz63nonpar in DeebLorenz have a vector field ff that is a polynomial of low degree. Thus, it is not surprising that methods based on this assumption, such as [SpPo](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodsppo "4th item ‣ 4th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") (polynomial solution smoother) and [SINDy](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodsindy "8th item ‣ 8th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") (similar to [SpPo](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodsppo "4th item ‣ 4th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), but assumes sparsity of target polynomial), perform well on these tasks. Note that a polynomial vector field ff does not imply that the propagator 𝒫Δ​t\mathcal{P}\_{\Delta\!t} for a given timestep Δ​t\Delta\!t is also polynomial. Still, there might be a reasonable polynomial approximation, which would explain the good performance of [Lin\*](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodlin "2nd item ‣ 2nd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") (ridge regression fit of polynomial propagator).

For Lorenz63std and Lorenz63random, the vector field ff is a quadratic polynomial. For these systems [SpPo2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodsppon "5th item ‣ 5th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), which fits such a polynomial, works very well (when excluding the extremely difficult combination of random timesteps and noisy observations). But the method shows poor performance for the non-polynomial Lorenz63nonpar. The same is true in the noisefree, constant timestep setting for methods that can fit higher degree polynomials ([SpPo](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodsppo "4th item ‣ 4th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), [SpPo4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodsppon "5th item ‣ 5th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), [SINDy](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodsindy "8th item ‣ 8th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), [SINDyN](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodsindy "8th item ‣ 8th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems")). In the noisy setting, where performance in general is worse, this effect is not visible, likely as a polynomial approximation (Taylor’s theorem) is accurate enough relative to the other methods.

The method [SINDyN](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodsindy "8th item ‣ 8th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") (with normalization) is usually worse than [SINDy](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodsindy "8th item ‣ 8th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"). This makes sense, as many systems studied here have sparse polynomial dynamics and normalization (which in our case includes a rotation) destroys sparsity.

All in all, low degree polynomial approximation works only well if the target function can be described sufficiently well as such a polynomial. Inherently nonparametric methods, such as [GpGp](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodgpgp "7th item ‣ 7th item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") or [PgGp\*](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodpg "1st item ‣ 1st item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), which both fit Gaussian processes, seem to be more suitable if the target is non-polynomial.

children.heading: 3.8 Choosing the Right Variant of Propagators Improves Performance

content.text: As expected, the errors of propagators with and without timestep input (\*T, [Table 15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A4.T15 "In Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems")) are similar when the timestep is constant. An exception is observed with [LinD](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodlin "2nd item ‣ 2nd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), [LinPo4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodlinpo "3rd item ‣ 3rd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), and [LinPo6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodlinpo "3rd item ‣ 3rd item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), which fit a polynomial propagator using ridge regression, in the noisefree case, where performance degrades when the timestep is (unnecessarily) included as an additional input. This decline is likely due to numerical issues arising from co-linear predictors. For random timesteps, however, providing timestep information improves the results in most cases.

Between the state (\*S\*) and the difference quotient (\*D\*) versions of the propagator estimators ([Table 16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A4.T16 "In Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems")), there is no clear overall winner. However, in the case of random timesteps without noise, difference-quotient based methods consistently yield lower errors. This may be due to the reduced dependence of the target on the timestep when estimating the difference quotient. Additionally, both [PgGp\*](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodpg "1st item ‣ 1st item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") and [PgNet\*](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodpg "1st item ‣ 1st item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), which fit the propagator map using a Gaussian process and a neural network, respectively, exhibit a clear preference for the difference quotient as the target (except in the noisy setting with random timesteps).

To explain this preference, note that system states change smoothly over time, so one-step-ahead predictions should be close to persistence (where future states equal the current state). When the target is the state, persistence is achieved by the identity function as the propagator. When the target is the difference quotient, persistence corresponds to the constant zero function. The Gaussian Process [PgGp\*](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodpg "1st item ‣ 1st item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") has a prior centered at zero, biasing it toward persistence in the difference quotient setup. In contrast, when the state is the target, its predictions are biased toward the mean of observations (climatology), as the input data is normalized. For the neural network [PgNet\*](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodpg "1st item ‣ 1st item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), the constant zero function is easier to learn since only the weights in the last layer need suitable values, while the identity function requires appropriate weights across all layers. Thus, both the Gaussian process and the neural network are better suited to the difference quotient setup due to their inherent bias towards zero.

children.heading: 3.9 Using The Cumulative Maximum Error Is Advantageous

content.text: When ranking different methods based on their performance, the error metrics 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME}, 𝗌𝖬𝖠𝖯𝖤\mathsf{sMAPE}, and t𝗏𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽t\_{\mathsf{valid}} generally produce similar results. However, a notable difference arises with 𝗌𝖬𝖠𝖯𝖤\mathsf{sMAPE} for more challenging tasks, where strong initial performance can be overshadowed by a divergence of the forecast later on (instead of, e.g., defaulting to a constant), see [Table 13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A4.T13 "In Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"). As seen from the explicit error values in [Table 14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A4.T14 "In Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), t𝗏𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽t\_{\mathsf{valid}} is less effective at distinguishing well-performing methods when the testing duration is too short or the threshold parameter is too lenient, as several methods can achieve the maximum valid time. The 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} does not suffer from any of these limitations.

children.heading: 3.10 Scarce Validation Data Can Lead to Over-Tuning

content.text: Unsurprisingly, the error measures of tuned methods typically perform better on the validation dataset than on the testing datasets, see [Table 14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A4.T14 "In Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"). For some methods, the difference is rather large (for the Echo State Network [EsnS](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodesn "1st item ‣ 1st item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), we have a median 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} of 0.00400.0040 on the noisefree Dysts validation data and 0.0300.030 on the test data). In combination with the high number of parameters tested for these methods (for [EsnS](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#methodesn "1st item ‣ 1st item ‣ 2.3 Estimation Methods ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") on the noisefree Dysts data, 288.5288.5 per system on average), this suggests that the hyperparameter tuning has the potential to introduce overfitting to the validation data. This affects Dysts more than DeebLorenz as there is much less tuning data for the former and no repetitions, making the validation errors less robust.

This study provides a comprehensive evaluation of various methods for time series prediction across several low-dimensional chaotic dynamical systems, demonstrating that lightweight, simple methods consistently outperform more complex, computationally intensive algorithms (see [Figure 6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S4.F6 "In 4 Conclusion ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems")). Methods based on the solution smoother approach or simple estimators of propagator maps showed both strong predictive performance and low computational costs. In contrast, more complex machine learning models that are trained using gradient descent generally underperformed.

Hyperparameter optimization is shown to be a key factor for improving accuracy in some methods, with optimized methods achieving errors several orders of magnitude lower than those reported in a previous study with limited tuning. Additionally, noise and random timestep designs were found to significantly impact performance, with different methods excelling under different conditions.

Furthermore, this work highlights the importance of robust evaluation practices. Repeating experiments is essential to ensure statistical significance. The use of appropriate error metrics, such as the newly introduced cumulative maximum error (𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME}), is necessary to capture relevant performance differences.

In general, meaningful evaluation of a method’s performance requires a carefully constructed study design that incorporates appropriate hyperparameter optimization, relevant baseline methods, informative error metrics, uncertainty quantification, and fair comparison practices. However, many existing studies fail to address one or more of these aspects, whereas we strive to adhere to these principles. Our findings challenge the increasing focus on complex, computationally intensive machine learning models and show that these models are often ill-suited for predicting low-dimensional chaotic systems. Instead, simpler and more efficient approaches tailored to the specific problem domain, frequently deliver superior performance.

The Dysts database consists of 133 chaotic systems with state space dimension between 33 and 1010, see [Table 4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A1.T4 "In A.1 Dysts ‣ Appendix A The Databases ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"). For a detailed description of the Dysts database, see [[Gil21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx9)]. Here we comment on some peculiarities of the database, in particular the noisy version.

1. (i) In the noisy version of the data, the system MacArthur is divergent (oscillating state values in the order of magnitude ±10100\pm 10^{100} and higher). Moreover, for CircadianRhythm and DoublePendulum, the variance of the solutions increases by multiple orders of magnitude between the noisefree and noisy version. 2. (ii) Curiously, the oscillating behavior of MacArthur makes this system rather predictable in the noisy case with a best 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} of 0.0550.055 achieved by EsnS, which is lower than the best noisefree 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} of 0.260.26 achieved by PgNetD. 3. (iii) For the noisefree testing dataset, the most difficult to learn systems seem to be LidDrivenCavityFlow, IkedaDelay, DoublePendulum, and ForcedVanDerPol. These all have values 0.85<𝖢𝖬𝖤<0.960.85<\mathsf{CME}<0.96 for the best methods in this study, while 100100 out of 133133 systems have a 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} below 0.10.1 for the best method. 4. (iv) For the following systems from the noisy testing dataset, learning seems impossible (best method with 𝖢𝖬𝖤>0.99\mathsf{CME}>0.99): ArnoldBeltramiChildress, ArnoldWeb, BickleyJet. Out of 133133 noisy systems, 2121 have a 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} below 0.10.1 and 1414 have a 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} above 0.90.9.

For propagator based methods, a mapping from the current state to the next one is learned. The target is either directly the next state (suffix S) or the increment scaled by the inverse of the time step (suffix D). The hyperparameter grids presented below are selected to perform well across all systems while maintaining bounded computational costs. Many advanced machine learning models, such as transformers, recurrent networks, and neural ODEs, have numerous variants. In this study, we employ standard, out-of-the-box architectures for all methods, applying minimal manual adjustments and relying on automatic hyperparameter tuning, as detailed below. While extensive fine-tuning of specific model variants could potentially improve performance for individual systems, our approach prioritizes fairness in comparison across models. This design also caters to practitioners with limited time and computational resources when applying machine learning to data from dynamical systems.

content.text: In this section, we show some mathematical properties of the symmetric mean absolute percent error, 𝗌𝖬𝖠𝖯𝖤\mathsf{sMAPE}.

chunks.text: # Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems

heading_path: Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems
chunks.text:
###### Abstract

Predicting chaotic dynamical systems is critical in many scientific fields, such as weather forecasting, but challenging due to the characteristic sensitive dependence on initial conditions. Traditional modeling approaches require extensive domain knowledge, often leading to a shift towards data-driven methods using machine learning. However, existing research provides inconclusive results on which machine learning methods are best suited for predicting chaotic systems. In this paper, we compare different lightweight and heavyweight machine learning architectures using extensive existing benchmark databases, as well as a newly introduced database that allows for uncertainty quantification in the benchmark results. In addition to state-of-the-art methods from the literature, we also present new advantageous variants of established methods. Hyperparameter tuning is adjusted based on computational cost, with more tuning allocated to less costly methods. Furthermore, we introduce the cumulative maximum error, a novel metric that combines desirable properties of traditional metrics and is tailored for chaotic systems. Our results show that well-tuned simple methods, as well as untuned baseline methods, often outperform state-of-the-art deep learning models, but their performance can vary significantly with different experimental setups. These findings highlight the importance of aligning prediction methods with data characteristics and caution against the indiscriminate use of overly complex models.

heading_path: Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems
chunks.text:
## 1 Introduction

Chaos is a ubiquitous phenomenon in nature and technology, arising from nonlinearities, complex interactions, or feedbacks within the system [[Ott02](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx19), [Str24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx32)]. Predicting the behavior of such dynamical systems is a critical goal in many scientific disciplines. Chaotic systems are characterized by their sensitive dependence on initial conditions, making them notoriously difficult to predict and posing a significant challenge to researchers studying them.

A traditional approach to addressing this problem involves using domain knowledge to model the dynamical system. However, this approach requires detailed understanding of the specific system that is often not be available. In recent years, system-agnostic, data-driven approaches have emerged as a viable alternative. These methods, which leverage techniques from statistics and machine learning, are trained on observational data to predict the future behavior of the system.

These algorithms range from relatively simple and computationally inexpensive methods, such as fitting polynomials, to highly sophisticated models that utilize complex neural network architectures, demanding significant computational power for training. To evaluate these approaches, various comparison studies have been conducted.

For instance, [[Han+21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx12)] focus on complex machine learning models with mostly classical neural network architectures. They do not include the sophisticated transformer model [[Vas+17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx33)], which has gained popularity due to its effectiveness for large language models. Such models are surveyed in [[Wen+23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx35)], where different variants of transformer models for time series forecasting are reviewed. Remarkably, [[Zen+23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx36)] demonstrate how simple linear methods can outperform these complex models. Additionally, [[Vla+20](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx34)] compare reservoir computers (RCs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), favoring RNNs, whereas [[SFC22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx29)] conduct a similar comparison, adding further machine learning methods and concluding that RCs are preferable.

Previous studies typically compare methods on a limited number of systems. However, [[Gil21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx9), [Gil23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx10)] emphasize the need to use extensive databases and benchmarks to evaluate the performance of different methods. They introduce a database of more than 130 different chaotic dynamical systems and, in their comparison study, find that the sophisticated NBEATS method [[Ore+20](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx18)] performs best. Hyperparameter tuning in this study is minimal, despite its importance for algorithm performance.

All in all, there is no consensus in the literature on which method should be preferred. Even a distinction in the quality of results between lightweight and heavyweight methods is not clear. Apart from using only a few systems (and often different data in each study), the lack of robustness of existing comparisons may stem from an inherent randomness in the evaluations. The results of the error metrics used may vary when different initial conditions are applied. If experiments are repeated only a few times with randomly drawn initial conditions, the results may still not be robust. If there is only one trial, then uncertainty cannot even be judged.

With this work, we aim to address several questions left open in previous studies. We compare various lightweight and heavyweight algorithms, including simple statistical methods that have shown promising performance but have received limited attention [[RH17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx23)]. We also present modifications of algorithms based on propagator map estimates, such as RCs, where we target the increment instead of the next state, and show the advantages of these for certain prediction tasks. We tune hyperparameters guided by the computational cost of each algorithm, allowing a broader exploration of hyperparameter sets for lightweight methods to facilitate a fairer comparison with heavyweight models.

As one source of synthetic data, we use the Dysts database of [[Gil21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx9)], allowing tests on a wide range of chaotic systems and direct comparison with the results in [[Gil23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx10)]. Additionally, we introduce a new database, DeebLorenz, which encompasses three variations of the well-known Lorenz63 system [[Lor63](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx17)], allowing for an easy comparison with other studies on the Lorenz63 system. Our database includes 100100 repetitions of simulated time series for each system to increase the robustness of results and to allow uncertainty quantification. The database also features a nonparametric version of Lorenz63 to assess the performance of polynomial-based fitting algorithms on non-polynomial targets. All the systems studied have state-space dimensions ranging from 33 to 1010, categorizing them as low-dimensional. Different observation schemes are used for each system to examine the impact of noise and time step intervals on performance. Furthermore, we propose a new error metric for forecasting tasks on dynamical systems, the cumulative maximum error (𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME}). It combines the benefits of integrated error metrics (as used in, e.g., [[Gil23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx10), [God+21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx11)]) and measures of forecast horizon, such as the valid time [[Ren+09](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx22), [Pat+18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx20)].

Our study demonstrates significantly better performance of various tuned and untuned simple methods compared to complex machine learning models on forecasting tasks for low-dimensional chaotic systems. Additionally, we find that the relative performance of methods is highly dependent on the experimental setup, though some trends, such as the strong performance of simple methods, remain consistent. Notably, introducing random time steps between consecutive observations dramatically alters performance. In this case, a Gaussian process-based method [[RW05](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx26), [Hei+18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#bib.bibx14)] that ranks mid-tier under constant time steps, outperforms all other methods.

The remaining parts of the paper are structured as follows: [Section 2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S2 "2 Methodology ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") describes the databases, the forecasting task, the methods compared, the 𝖢𝖬𝖤\mathsf{CME} error metric, and the hyperparameter tuning. The results and key insights of the simulation study are described in [Section 3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S3 "3 Results and 10 Key Insights ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"), followed by a short conclusion in [Section 4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#S4 "4 Conclusion ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"). [Appendix A](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A1 "Appendix A The Databases ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems") provides additional details on the databases, followed by a discussion of the estimation methods in [Appendix B](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A2 "Appendix B Methods ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems"). Finally, additional tables and plots detailing the simulation study results are available in [Appendix D](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.20158#A4 "Appendix D Further Details of the Results ‣ Machine Learning for Predicting Chaotic Systems").

### 2.2 Prediction Task and Evaluation

For all systems, observation schemes, datasets, and repetitions, we impose the following task: Given the observations of the past, (ti,Yi)i=1,…,n(t\_{i},Y\_{i})\_{i=1,\dots,n} in the time interval ti∈[0,T]t\_{i}\in[0,T] (training time), and the true current state u⁡(T)u(T), predict the future states u⁡(tj)u(t\_{j}) at given times tj∈[T,T+S]t\_{j}\in[T,T+S] (prediction time) for j=1,…,mj=1,\dots,m.

ti∈[0,T]t_{i}\in[0,T]

u⁡(tj)u(t_{j})

tj∈[T,T+S]t_{j}\in[T,T+S]

Allowing the forecasting methods to know the true current state u⁡(T)u(T) — even in the case of otherwise noisy observations — eliminates the dependence of our simulation results on the (random) specific noise value of the final observation. This is crucial to increase the reliability of our comparison study, since prediction errors in chaotic systems typically grow exponentially with time. Additionally, it allows us to concentrate solely on the forecasting task (predicting future states) rather than on the data assimilation task (estimating the true value of a nosily observed state).
